_README: i18n probe fixture — a fixed, model-agnostic test set for hi and tr.
Both runs receive this EXACT input so the comparison is apples-to-apples.
Validate any run's answer with:  python3 tooling/i18n_probe_validate.py <lang> <answers.json>
The validator checks STRUCTURE only (what can be checked mechanically):
- placeholders: every %(name)s multiset must equal the English source
- ids / urls / pinned keys: must survive byte-verbatim
- line count: multi-line values keep their line count
- script contamination: hi output must contain no Latin/Cyrillic/CJK runs
tr output must contain no Devanagari/Cyrillic/CJK runs
- loanwords: declared allowlist, so every Latin token is a visible decision
Structure passing does NOT mean the translation is good. Meaning, register and
morphology are for a human or a stronger model to judge — that is the point of
the side-by-side. The `why` field names the specific failure each item probes.

items.why: Hindi: postposition + verb agreement; dropping 'your' loses the security subject. Turkish: dative case on the wallet, imperative register.
Hindi: infinitive 'to sign' plus purposive clause. Turkish: 'sign' is a loanword; the verb is the hard part.
Bare label. Hindi often borrows 'पासवर्ड'; Turkish commonly does too. A wrong choice here reads as untrustworthy.
Technical noun phrase with an English loanword component. Both languages typically keep 'algorithm' or transliterate it.
Parenthetical with a clause. The numeric prefix must stay a numeric prefix and not be reordered into prose.
Two-parenthetical technical label; '+' is a structural symbol and must survive. Hindi: stacked postpositions in the parenthetical.

items.en: auto-disable time must be in the future.
items.why: Modal obligation + temporal condition. Turkish stacks case and copula; Hindi needs correct postposition order (में after the noun phrase).
Short technical error with a modal verb. Error strings are where fluency looks best and meaning is most easily lost.

items.en: Amount must be greater than zero.
items.why: Validation rule. If the comparison direction is inverted the user is told the opposite of the truth.
Past participle + 'and' + technical verb. 'broadcast' is a domain term; a mistranslation here implies the tx did not go out.
Four placeholders, an em dash and a middle dot. Structural checker must prove all four survive and the separators are not reordered.
Placeholder inside a parenthetical with a trailing period outside it. Punctuation placement must survive the case stack.
Bare 'X / Y' count display. The slash and spacing are load-bearing; over-translating this is a common failure.
En-dash range + placeholder + two sentences. The en dash must not become a hyphen or a word.

items.en: Broadcast unavailable: the op-34 serializer is not loaded in this bundle (tx.js/tx-send.js).
items.why: Contains op number 34 AND file paths that MUST stay byte-verbatim. A model that 'translates' tx.js breaks a real reference.

items.en:
# Publishing price feeds
Publish the settlement price for a market-pegged asset from the [Issue desk](#/assets/feed).
items.why: Markdown: heading line, body line, and a link whose hash MUST survive while its label is translated. Line count is 2.
'legs' is domain jargon (price feed legs). Both languages borrow it; over-literal translation loses the domain meaning.
Bare past participle used as a status value. Hindi/Turkish both have distinct perfective forms; the wrong aspect reads as 'is authorizing'.

items.en: Show the English reference for this line
items.why: An aria-label read ALOUD at every signing line. Must be short enough to speak and must not lose 'English'.

items.en: These translations were written by a machine and have not been checked by a human. The English text is always one tap away on any line marked with *.
items.why: THE honesty string. If this is unclear, a reader cannot know their translation is unverified. Longest and most important item here.
